P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes. Export of services is governed by RBI's Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, in force from 1 October 2026; they replace the 2015 regulations. 'Services' includes 'software', defined broadly as any computer programme, database, drawing, design, audio/video signals or any information delivered other than on a physical medium. So digital products count. The full export value must be realised and repatriated within NINE months from the invoice date, or twelve months if invoiced or settled in Indian rupees. This was amended on 22 September 2026: the text previously said fifteen and eighteen months. Exporters file an EDF declaration with their bank within 30 days after the invoice month, or for non-software services on or before the payment date. Invoices up to ₹10 lakh can be closed in the bank's EDPMS system on the exporter's declaration.

The old Master Direction on Export of Goods and Services (2016, nine months) is superseded.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can individuals hold a foreign-currency bank account?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Any person resident in India may open an Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency (EEFC) account with an authorised dealer bank and credit 100% of foreign-exchange earnings received through banking channels. The account is a non-interest-bearing current account. Funds can pay for permitted current and capital account transactions abroad, and there is no restriction on withdrawing them in rupees. Resident individuals can add resident relatives as joint holders on a former-or-survivor basis. The current regulation text (amended up to 9 October 2025) does not contain the old rule requiring conversion to rupees by the end of the following month.

P4_paypal.question: PayPal capability in the country
P4_paypal.answer: PayPal operates in India for EXPORT receipts only. Under PayPal India's user agreement (last updated 13 Jan 2025), the service lets residents receive payments from buyers outside India for exported goods and services. PayPal deposits the proceeds with an authorised dealer bank, so the money goes to your Indian bank account; PayPal does not hold it for you. Using Export Payment Services for a product or service worth more than USD 10,000 per transaction is a restricted activity. An RBI purpose code must be set before you can withdraw, and it decides whether you need an IEC (Importer Exporter Code). PayPal's Payouts table lists India as 'Receive and withdraw' only.

P5_payoneer_wise.question: Payoneer / Wise availability for residents
P5_payoneer_wise.answer: Payoneer: available. Payoneer's India guide (last modified 31 Aug 2026) says it complies with FEMA, asks for government ID such as Aadhaar or PAN plus proof of an Indian bank account, and lets you withdraw in INR to an Indian bank. Wise: receiving is for business customers only, but Wise onboards 'Sole trader / freelancer' as a business type: you earn as an individual, and your PAN and receiving bank account are in your personal name. You get account details in 24 currencies, including local USD, GBP and EUR. Funds are auto-converted to INR and sent to your Indian bank, and can't be held in Wise balances or used to send money. Limits are USD 5 minimum and ₹2.5M maximum per transaction. Aadhaar and PAN are verified by video KYC while you are physically in India.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual selling digital products or services register a business? How (sole proprietor), cost, online?
L1_registration.answer: No separate business registration is required. Startup India (DPIIT) says there is no separate registration procedure for proprietorships; they are recognised through other registrations, such as tax registration, relevant to the business. Optional: Udyam (MSME) registration on the official portal is free, paperless and based on self-declaration. PAN- and GST-linked figures are pulled automatically, and GSTIN is required only where the CGST Act applies. Other registrations depend on the business: GST (see L4), possibly a state Shops & Establishments licence (not checked), and IEC for exporting goods (PayPal ties this to the purpose code, see P4).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: How residents' foreign-sourced or digital income is taxed
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: From 1 April 2026 the Income Tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act, which is repealed. Income from FY 2026-27 is 'Tax Year 2026-27'; anything before that stays under the 1961 Act. Residents must report all income from sources outside India in Schedule FSI, claim foreign tax credit under the relevant DTAA in Schedule TR, and disclose all foreign assets and accounts in Schedule FA, unless they are 'not ordinarily resident'. Presumptive scheme for professionals, verified only under the OLD Act for FY 2025-26 (s.44ADA): income declared at 50% of gross receipts with no books required. Eligible if receipts are up to ₹75 lakh (when cash receipts are at most 5%), otherwise ₹50 lakh, for professions listed in s.44AA(1). Under the new Act these schemes are consolidated into section 58, but the new thresholds and rates were not verified because the Act text was blocked (see notes).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported services and digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: GST. Exports of goods or services are 'zero rated supplies' (IGST Act s.16). A registered exporter can supply under a bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT, FORM GST RFD-11) without paying integrated tax and claim a refund of unused input tax credit. Registration: people making inter-State supplies of taxable services (exports count as inter-State supplies under IGST s.7(5)(a)) are exempt from registration while their all-India aggregate turnover stays at or below ₹20 lakh a year, or ₹10 lakh in special category States (Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax). Domestic sales to Indian customers above the threshold are taxable; the current domestic rate for IT services was not verified (see notes).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law: name, year, in force?, regulator
L5_data_protection.answer: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act). Its DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 14 November 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline. The regulator is the Data Protection Board of India: fully digital, four members, appeals to TDSAT. Penalties reach up to ₹200 crore, for example for failing to notify the Board or affected individuals of a personal data breach. Small sellers handling Indian customers' data are data fiduciaries under the Act.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: E-commerce / consumer-protection law relevant to online sales
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 plus the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. The Rules cover all goods and services bought or sold over a digital or electronic network, digital products included. An 'e-commerce entity' is anyone who owns, operates or manages a platform for electronic commerce. That includes a person selling from their own website or app, but not a seller on someone else's marketplace (marketplace sellers have separate duties). Every e-commerce entity must set up a grievance mechanism and appoint and display a grievance officer, who acknowledges complaints within 48 hours and resolves them within one month. Amendment Rules 2026 (published Sept 2026) add ranking-transparency and display duties, but their commencement date could not be read reliably (see notes).

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Receive and withdraw'). (6) Stripe lists this country as 'Preview' (sign-up by contacting Stripe sales), which is not a self-serve route for beginners yet. (7) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (8) Local official channel: Credit 100% of foreign earnings to an EEFC account (RBI), or withdraw from Payoneer in INR to an Indian bank (P2/P5). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
